rationale: A wins because it has the cleaner editor brain: it knows the strongest story is not the sensor launch, it is "Eight Sleep puts blood-oxygen and snoring tracking behind its top subscription tier," and it keeps the regulatory, audience, and trend angles in separate lanes. B is solid, but it gets sloppy at the edges: "a live clinical study with an unnamed sleep clinic" contradicts the update's named clinic fact, and "health-equity reporter" overreaches from premium pricing into a heavier beat it has not earned. This is not a blowout; B has real shapes, but A is tighter, meaner about proof, and less likely to get the founder in trouble.
gaps_in_A: "A mattress that watches your breathing and changes its own temperature while you sleep" is the weakest angle; without competitor proof it admits it may collapse into a product-feature description.
"Why athletes and biohackers are the test market" needs an actual named user; A flags that honestly, but the angle remains thin until that proof exists.
The clinical-study partnership is mostly treated as a regulatory-background fact, but A could more explicitly say the named clinic is unusable as validation until results exist.
gaps_in_B: "a live clinical study with an unnamed sleep clinic" is wrong against the update, which says the study is with a named sleep clinic. Small word, bad signal.
"health-equity reporter" is a stretch; premium wellness hardware pricing is not automatically a health-equity story without access data or affected populations.
"Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time" is category puff unless supported by other examples, which B itself admits it does not have.
The next step says "find-journalists" across four viable shapes, but the sharper move is to pick the subscription or regulatory angle first and run fit-check from there.
